transitivity: both — transitive (accelerate the car), intransitive (the train accelerated)
gloss: To go faster, or to make something go faster.
examples: This car *accelerates* from zero to sixty in six seconds.
She *accelerated* to pass the truck.
He was *accelerating* when a deer stepped onto the road.

transitivity: transitive
gloss: To go somewhere together with someone.
examples: A guide *accompanies* every group into the canyon.
Her brother *accompanied* her to the airport.
Children under twelve must be *accompanied* by an adult.
contrast: Consonant + *-y* changes: *accompany → accompanies, accompanied*, but *accompanying* keeps the *y*.

transitivity: both — transitive (advance the ball), intransitive (the line advanced)
gloss: To move forward, especially steadily or with effort.
examples: The line *advances* about one person a minute.
The troops *advanced* under cover of darkness.
Storm clouds were *advancing* from the west.

transitivity: intransitive
gloss: To reach the place you were traveling to.
examples: Our flight *arrives* at six in the morning.
We *arrived* in Denver two hours late.
The package still has not *arrived*.
contrast: *arrive **in*** a city or country, *arrive **at*** a building or a point. Never *arrive to*.

transitivity: both — transitive (ascend the stairs), intransitive (the balloon ascended)
gloss: To go up to a higher place.
examples: The trail *ascends* steeply for the first mile.
The balloon *ascended* until it disappeared.
We spent the morning *ascending* the ridge.

transitivity: both — transitive (board the train), intransitive (we boarded at gate 12)
gloss: To get on a plane, train, ship, or bus.
examples: Passengers in group C may now *board*.
We *boarded* the ferry just before it pulled away.
They have already *boarded* the plane.

transitivity: both — transitive (bounce a ball), intransitive (the ball bounced)
gloss: To spring back after hitting a surface, or to make something do that.
examples: He *bounces* the ball while he thinks.
The ball *bounced* twice and rolled into the street.
The kids have been *bouncing* on the bed all morning.

transitivity: intransitive
gloss: To slow down or stop a vehicle by using the brakes.
examples: He *brakes* too late on wet roads.
She *braked* hard when the light turned red.
The truck was *braking* all the way down the hill.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *break* (сломать). The silent *-e* drops before *-ing*: *braking*.

transitivity: transitive
gloss: To hold something and move it from one place to another.
examples: Let me *carry* that bag for you.
She *carried* the sleeping child upstairs.
He was *carrying* two suitcases and a cup of coffee.
contrast: Consonant + *-y* changes: *carry → carries, carried*, but *carrying* keeps the *y*.

transitivity: transitive
gloss: To run after someone or something in order to catch them.
examples: The dog *chases* every squirrel in the yard.
Police *chased* the car for three miles.
She spent the afternoon *chasing* a toddler around the park.

transitivity: both — transitive (circle the airport), intransitive (hawks circled overhead)
gloss: To move all the way around something.
examples: Hawks *circle* above that field every evening.
The plane *circled* the airport for twenty minutes.
We kept *circling* the block looking for parking.

transitivity: intransitive
gloss: To hit something violently while moving.
examples: Meteors *collide* with the atmosphere and burn up.
Two cars *collided* at the intersection this morning.
The bus had *collided* with a guardrail before it stopped.
contrast: *collide **with*** something.

ru: ездить на работу и обратно, добираться
transitivity: intransitive
gloss: To travel regularly between your home and your job.
examples: I *commute* forty minutes each way.
She *commuted* into the city for eleven years.
He has been *commuting* by train since March.

transitivity: both — transitive (continue the trip), intransitive (the road continues)
gloss: To keep going without stopping.
examples: *Continue* straight for two miles, then turn right.
The road *continued* past the last farmhouse.
The rain has *continued* all night.

transitivity: both — transitive (crash the car), intransitive (the plane crashed)
gloss: To hit something hard and be damaged, especially in a vehicle.
examples: Planes rarely *crash*, but people still worry.
He *crashed* his bike into a mailbox.
A truck had *crashed* on the on-ramp, so we sat there for an hour.
contrast: *crash **into*** something. Third person adds *-es*: *crashes*.

transitivity: intransitive
gloss: To move forward on your hands and knees, or to move very slowly.
examples: The baby *crawls* everywhere now.
We *crawled* under the fence.
Traffic was *crawling* along at five miles an hour.

transitivity: both — transitive (cross the street), intransitive (cross at the light)
gloss: To go from one side of something to the other.
examples: Look both ways before you *cross*.
We *crossed* the border a little after noon.
They have *crossed* that river three times today.
contrast: Third person adds *-es* after *-ss*: *crosses*.

ru: путешествовать на теплоходе; ехать не спеша
transitivity: both — transitive (cruise the coast), intransitive (the plane cruises)
gloss: To travel smoothly at a steady speed, especially by ship or car.
examples: The plane *cruises* at thirty-five thousand feet.
We *cruised* down the coast with the windows open.
They spent a week *cruising* the Caribbean.

transitivity: intransitive
gloss: To run somewhere very quickly and for a short distance.
examples: He *dashes* out for coffee every morning at ten.
She *dashed* across the platform and caught the train.
I was *dashing* to the gate when they called my name.

transitivity: transitive
gloss: To take goods or mail to the place where they were sent.
examples: They *deliver* between nine and noon.
The driver *delivered* the package to the wrong door.
We are *delivering* the furniture on Thursday.
contrast: Stress is on the middle syllable, so the *r* is not doubled: *delivered, delivering*.

transitivity: both — transitive (depart the station), intransitive (the train departed)
gloss: To leave, especially on a scheduled trip.
examples: The last bus *departs* at eleven forty.
We *departed* an hour behind schedule.
The ship was *departing* as we ran down the dock.
contrast: *depart **from*** a place. It is the formal opposite of *arrive*.

transitivity: both — transitive (descend the stairs), intransitive (the plane descended)
gloss: To move down to a lower place.
examples: The plane began to *descend* over the lake.
We *descended* the stairs in the dark.
Fog was *descending* on the whole valley.

transitivity: both — transitive (dock the boat), intransitive (the ferry docked)
gloss: To bring a boat to a dock, or to arrive at one.
examples: The ferry *docks* every hour on the hour.
Our ship *docked* in Miami at dawn.
They were still *docking* when the storm hit.

transitivity: transitive
gloss: To pull something heavy along the ground.
examples: Do not *drag* the couch across the floor.
He *dragged* the trash cans out to the curb.
She was *dragging* a suitcase with a broken wheel.
contrast: One vowel + one consonant, so the *g* doubles: *dragged, dragging*.

transitivity: intransitive
gloss: To be carried slowly along by water, air, or a current.
examples: We let the canoe *drift* for a while.
The raft *drifted* two miles downstream overnight.
Leaves were *drifting* across the empty road.

transitivity: both — transitive (drop the keys), intransitive (the temperature dropped)
gloss: To let something fall, or to fall suddenly.
examples: Be careful not to *drop* the eggs.
She *dropped* her keys through the grate.
The temperature has *dropped* twenty degrees since noon.
contrast: One vowel + one consonant, so the *p* doubles: *dropped, dropping*.

ru: садиться на судно; отправляться в путь
transitivity: intransitive
gloss: To get on a ship or plane, or to start a journey.
examples: Passengers *embark* at the south terminal.
We *embarked* in Seattle on a rainy morning.
They are *embarking* on a year-long trip around Asia.
contrast: *embark **on*** a journey or a project.

transitivity: transitive
gloss: To go with someone in order to guide or protect them.

Two police cars *escorted* the convoy.
She was *escorted* through the crowd by security.

transitivity: transitive
gloss: To get away from someone who is chasing or looking for you.
examples: Deer *evade* hunters by moving at night.
The suspect *evaded* police for six days.
He has *evaded* capture twice already.

transitivity: both — transitive (exit the building), intransitive (exit at the next ramp)
gloss: To go out of a place, or to leave a highway.
examples: *Exit* at the next ramp and turn left.
We *exited* the theater through a side door.
Cars were *exiting* onto the service road.
contrast: Stress is on the first syllable, so the *t* is not doubled: *exited, exiting*.

transitivity: both — transitive (explore the caves), intransitive (we explored on foot)
gloss: To travel through an unfamiliar place in order to learn about it.
examples: Let us *explore* the old part of town.
They *explored* the caves with headlamps.
We spent Saturday *exploring* the coast road.

transitivity: transitive
gloss: To carry people or goods across water or over a short distance.
examples: A small boat *ferries* hikers to the island.
His dad *ferried* us to practice every Tuesday.
Helicopters were *ferrying* supplies to the flooded town.
contrast: Consonant + *-y* changes: *ferry → ferries, ferried*, but *ferrying* keeps the *y*.

transitivity: both — transitive (float a log downstream), intransitive (wood floats)
gloss: To stay on the surface of a liquid, or to move gently through the air.
examples: Wood *floats*, stone does not.
The raft *floated* downstream all afternoon.
Balloons were *floating* over the parking lot.

transitivity: intransitive
gloss: To move steadily and continuously, the way a liquid does.
examples: The river *flows* south into the bay.
Traffic *flowed* smoothly once the extra lane opened.
Water was *flowing* across the road.

transitivity: both — transitive (follow me), intransitive (you go first, I will follow)
gloss: To go after or behind someone or something.
examples: *Follow* me, I know a shortcut.
A gray car *followed* us for a few blocks.
The dog has been *following* him around all day.

transitivity: intransitive
gloss: To move smoothly and quietly without visible effort.
examples: Skaters *glide* across that pond all winter.
The canoe *glided* under the bridge.
A hawk was *gliding* on the warm air above the field.

transitivity: transitive
gloss: To show someone the way by going with them.
examples: A ranger will *guide* you to the falls.
She *guided* us through the market.
He has been *guiding* rafting trips for ten years.

transitivity: both — transitive (halt the traffic), intransitive (the convoy halted)
gloss: To stop moving, or to make something stop.
examples: Snow *halts* traffic on this pass every year.
The convoy *halted* at the checkpoint.
Work has been *halted* until the inspection is done.

transitivity: transitive
gloss: To pull or carry something heavy over a distance.

We *hauled* the canoe up the bank.
He was *hauling* firewood all morning.

transitivity: intransitive
gloss: To go in a particular direction.
examples: We *head* out at six tomorrow.
She *headed* straight for the exit.
Storm clouds were *heading* our way.
contrast: *head **for*** or *head **toward*** a place.

ru: ходить в поход, идти пешком (по горам, лесу)
transitivity: both — transitive (hike the ridge), intransitive (we hiked all day)
gloss: To take a long walk in the country or the mountains.
examples: We *hike* that ridge every fall.
They *hiked* eleven miles in one day.
She has been *hiking* since she was a kid.

transitivity: intransitive
gloss: To jump on one foot or in short light jumps, or to get quickly on or off something.
examples: *Hop* in, I will drive you.
The rabbit *hopped* across the yard.
He was *hopping* on one foot after the game.
contrast: One vowel + one consonant, so the *p* doubles: *hopped, hopping*. Compare *hope → hoped, hoping*.

transitivity: intransitive
gloss: To stay in one place in the air.
examples: Hummingbirds *hover* while they feed.
A helicopter *hovered* over the freeway.
The drone was *hovering* just above the roof.

transitivity: both — transitive (hurry the kids along), intransitive (we hurried)
gloss: To move or do something more quickly than usual.
examples: *Hurry* or we will miss the train.
She *hurried* down the platform.
They were *hurrying* to finish before the rain.
contrast: Consonant + *-y* changes: *hurry → hurries, hurried*, but *hurrying* keeps the *y*.

transitivity: intransitive
gloss: To run slowly and steadily for exercise.
examples: I *jog* three mornings a week.
He *jogged* around the reservoir.
She was *jogging* when the storm started.
contrast: One vowel + one consonant, so the *g* doubles: *jogged, jogging*.

transitivity: both — transitive (jump the fence), intransitive (he jumped)
gloss: To push yourself off the ground with your legs.
examples: Do not *jump* off that wall.
He *jumped* over the puddle.
The kids have been *jumping* in the leaves.

transitivity: both — transitive (land the plane), intransitive (we landed on time)
gloss: To come down onto the ground after being in the air.
examples: The plane *lands* at four fifteen.
We *landed* in Chicago in a snowstorm.
A bird was *landing* on the wire outside.

transitivity: transitive
gloss: To send something into the air or the water, or to start it moving.
examples: They *launch* the boat from the ramp.
NASA *launched* the rocket at dawn.
Crews were *launching* rescue boats all night.
contrast: Third person adds *-es* after *-ch*: *launches*.

transitivity: both — transitive (lift the box), intransitive (the fog lifted)
gloss: To raise something to a higher position.
examples: Can you *lift* the other end?
He *lifted* the bike onto the rack.
She was *lifting* boxes into the truck all morning.

transitivity: intransitive
gloss: To walk with difficulty because one leg hurts.
examples: She still *limps* a little in cold weather.
He *limped* off the field.
The dog was *limping* after the long walk.

transitivity: both — transitive (load the truck), intransitive (we loaded up and left)
gloss: To put things into or onto a vehicle or a container.
examples: Help me *load* the car.
They *loaded* the truck in twenty minutes.
We were still *loading* when the movers arrived.

transitivity: transitive
gloss: To send something through the postal system.
examples: I will *mail* the forms tomorrow.
She *mailed* the package on Friday.
They have already *mailed* the tickets.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *male*.

transitivity: both — transitive (march the prisoners out), intransitive (the band marched)
gloss: To walk with regular steps, especially as part of a group.
examples: The band *marches* onto the field at halftime.
Thousands *marched* down the avenue.
Soldiers were *marching* past the gate.
contrast: Third person adds *-es* after *-ch*: *marches*.

ru: вливаться, влиться; перестраиваться в общий поток
transitivity: both — transitive (merge the two lanes), intransitive (merge onto the highway)
gloss: To join a line of moving traffic, or to combine into one.
examples: *Merge* carefully, that lane ends soon.
He *merged* onto the highway without signaling.
Two lanes were *merging* into one.
contrast: *merge **onto*** a highway, *merge **with*** something.

transitivity: intransitive
gloss: To move from one region to another, usually with the seasons.
examples: Geese *migrate* south every fall.
His family *migrated* west during the Depression.
Whales are *migrating* along the coast right now.

transitivity: both — transitive (move the car), intransitive (the line moved)
gloss: To change place or position, or to go and live somewhere else.
examples: Please *move* your car.
They *moved* to Portland last spring.
The line has not *moved* in ten minutes.

transitivity: both — transitive (navigate the channel), intransitive (you drive, I will navigate)
gloss: To find the way when traveling, or to steer a ship or plane.
examples: You drive and I will *navigate*.
They *navigated* by the stars.
She was *navigating* from a paper map.

transitivity: both — transitive (pace the hallway), intransitive (he paced nervously)
gloss: To walk back and forth in the same small space.
examples: She *paces* whenever she is on the phone.
He *paced* the hallway outside the room.
They were *pacing* the waiting room for hours.

transitivity: both — transitive (pack a bag), intransitive (I still have to pack)
gloss: To put your things into a bag or a box before a trip.
examples: I still have to *pack*.
She *packed* two sweaters and a raincoat.
He was *packing* at midnight the night before the flight.

transitivity: both — transitive (paddle a canoe), intransitive (we paddled upstream)
gloss: To move a small boat through water with a paddle.
examples: They *paddle* the same river every summer.
We *paddled* across the lake before sunrise.
He was *paddling* hard against the current.

transitivity: both — transitive (park the car), intransitive (park in the back)
gloss: To leave a vehicle somewhere for a period of time.
examples: You cannot *park* here on Tuesdays.
She *parked* two blocks away.
We have been *parking* in the garage all week.

transitivity: both — transitive (pass the truck), intransitive (a car passed on the right)
gloss: To go by someone or something, or to move past it.
examples: We *pass* the lake on the way home.
A truck *passed* us on the right.
They were *passing* through Ohio when the call came.
contrast: Third person adds *-es*: *passes*. The past form *passed* sounds exactly like *past*.

ru: делать паузу, приостанавливаться, остановиться на миг
transitivity: both — transitive (pause the video), intransitive (she paused at the door)
gloss: To stop for a short time before going on.
examples: He *pauses* before every answer.
She *paused* at the top of the stairs.
They were *pausing* every few minutes to rest.

transitivity: both — transitive (pedal a bike), intransitive (he pedaled uphill)
gloss: To push the pedals of a bicycle to make it move.
examples: *Pedal* faster up this part.
He *pedaled* the last mile standing up.
She was *pedaling* into a headwind.
contrast: American spelling keeps one *l*: *pedaled, pedaling* (British *pedalled, pedalling*). Do not confuse with *peddle* (торговать вразнос).

transitivity: intransitive
gloss: To go on to the next place or the next step.

transitivity: both — transitive (pull the door), intransitive (pull harder)

She was *pulling* a wagon full of kids.

transitivity: transitive
gloss: To follow someone in order to catch or reach them.

Two patrol cars *pursued* the van across town.
Officers were *pursuing* the suspect on foot.

transitivity: both — transitive (push the cart), intransitive (push harder)
gloss: To move something away from you by pressing on it.
examples: *Push* the cart over here.
He *pushed* the stalled car off the road.
She was *pushing* a stroller up the hill.
contrast: Third person adds *-es* after *-sh*: *pushes*.

transitivity: both — transitive (race him to the corner), intransitive (he raced home)
gloss: To move very fast, or to compete for speed.
examples: Do not *race* down the stairs.
He *raced* to the gate and just made it.
They were *racing* each other to the mailbox.

transitivity: both — transitive (relocate the office), intransitive (they relocated to Arizona)
gloss: To move to a different place to live or work.
examples: The company wants to *relocate* him to Austin.
They *relocated* to Arizona after he retired.
We are *relocating* the office next month.

transitivity: intransitive
gloss: To stay in the same place instead of leaving.
examples: Please *remain* seated until we reach the gate.
She *remained* on the platform until the train was out of sight.
Only three passengers have *remained* on board.

transitivity: transitive
gloss: To take something away from a place.
examples: Please *remove* your bags from the aisle.
They *removed* the roadblock at noon.
Snow has been *removed* from the main roads.

transitivity: intransitive
gloss: To move back away from a difficult or dangerous place.
examples: Glaciers *retreat* a little further every year.
The army *retreated* across the river.
We were *retreating* to the car as the rain started.

transitivity: both — transitive (return the keys), intransitive (they returned late)
gloss: To come or go back to a place, or to give something back.
examples: They *return* from Spain on Sunday.
He *returned* to the same hotel every summer.
She has not *returned* my call.

ru: ехать задним ходом, сдавать назад; менять на противоположное
transitivity: both — transitive (reverse the car), intransitive (he reversed slowly)
gloss: To drive backward, or to turn something the opposite way.
examples: *Reverse* slowly, the driveway is narrow.
He *reversed* into a parking space.
The truck was *reversing* when it hit the pole.

transitivity: both — transitive (roam the hills), intransitive (cattle roam free)
gloss: To move around a wide area without a fixed direction.
examples: Cattle *roam* the whole valley.
We *roamed* the old city for hours.
A stray dog had been *roaming* the neighborhood for weeks.

transitivity: both — transitive (roll the barrel), intransitive (the ball rolled)
gloss: To move by turning over and over, or to make something do that.
examples: Waves *roll* in all afternoon.
The ball *rolled* under the car.
He was *rolling* the barrel toward the truck.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *role* (роль).

transitivity: both — transitive (rotate the tires), intransitive (the Earth rotates)
gloss: To turn around a center point.
examples: The Earth *rotates* once a day.
He *rotated* the tires before the trip.
The beam was *rotating* slowly above the harbor.

transitivity: both — transitive (row the boat), intransitive (they row every morning)
gloss: To move a boat through water using oars.

transitivity: both — transitive (rush him to the hospital), intransitive (do not rush)
gloss: To go somewhere or do something very quickly.
examples: Do not *rush*, we have time.
They *rushed* him to the hospital.

ru: плыть на судне, идти под парусом; отплывать
transitivity: both — transitive (sail the coast), intransitive (we sail at dawn)
gloss: To travel on water in a boat or a ship.

transitivity: both — transitive (scatter the seed), intransitive (the birds scattered)
gloss: To move apart quickly in different directions, or to throw things around.

transitivity: both — transitive (shift the couch), intransitive (the wind shifted)

transitivity: both — transitive (ship the order), intransitive (we ship on Mondays)

transitivity: both — transitive (shuttle guests to the airport), intransitive (he shuttled between two offices)

transitivity: both — transitive (signal a turn), intransitive (signal before you merge)
gloss: To show which way you are turning, or to give someone a sign.

transitivity: intransitive
gloss: To slide sideways on a road after losing grip.

transitivity: both — transitive (skip a stone), intransitive (she skipped down the street)
gloss: To move along with light hops from one foot to the other.

She *skipped* down the sidewalk.
He was *skipping* stones across the water.
contrast: One vowel + one consonant, so the *p* doubles: *skipped, skipping*.

transitivity: both — transitive (slip the note under the door), intransitive (he slipped on the ice)
gloss: To slide by accident and lose your balance, or to move quietly.

He *slipped* on the wet steps.
She was *slipping* out the back door when we saw her.

transitivity: intransitive
gloss: To fly high in the air without much effort.

Gulls were *soaring* on the wind off the water.

transitivity: intransitive
gloss: To run as fast as you can for a short distance.
examples: She *sprints* the last hundred meters.

transitivity: both — transitive (stalk the deer), intransitive (the cat stalked closer)

transitivity: intransitive
gloss: To remain in a place instead of leaving.
examples: *Stay* here while I get the car.
We *stayed* in a motel outside town.
They have been *staying* with friends since the flood.
contrast: Vowel + *-y* keeps the *y*: *stayed*, never *staid*.

transitivity: both — transitive (steer the boat), intransitive (he steers with one hand)
gloss: To control the direction of a vehicle or a boat.
examples: This boat *steers* better with two people aboard.
He *steered* with one hand.
She was *steering* while he read the map.

transitivity: intransitive
gloss: To move by putting one foot down in a new place.
examples: *Step* back from the platform edge.
She *stepped* over the puddle.
He was *stepping* off the curb when the bike went by.
contrast: One vowel + one consonant, so the *p* doubles: *stepped, stepping*.

transitivity: both — transitive (stop the car), intransitive (the bus stopped)
gloss: To end movement, or to make something end.
examples: The bus *stops* at every corner.
We *stopped* for gas outside Barstow.
It has not *stopped* raining since Tuesday.
contrast: One vowel + one consonant, so the *p* doubles: *stopped, stopping*. Compare *hope → hoped, hoping*.

transitivity: intransitive
gloss: To wander away from the right place or path.
examples: Do not *stray* from the trail.
The dog *strayed* into the neighbor's yard.
A few sheep had *strayed* onto the road.

transitivity: intransitive
gloss: To walk slowly and in a relaxed way.
examples: They *stroll* through the park after dinner.
We *strolled* along the waterfront.
An old couple was *strolling* ahead of us.

transitivity: intransitive
gloss: To hit your foot on something and almost fall.
examples: People *stumble* on that step all the time.
He *stumbled* on a loose brick.
She was *stumbling* in the dark without a flashlight.

transitivity: transitive
gloss: To be or move all around something on every side.
examples: Mountains *surround* the town.
Police *surrounded* the building.
The house is *surrounded* by tall pines.

transitivity: intransitive
gloss: To turn suddenly to one side while moving.
examples: The bus *swerves* around that pothole every day.
He *swerved* to miss a deer.
A car was *swerving* between lanes ahead of us.

transitivity: intransitive
gloss: To walk quietly on the front part of your feet.
examples: *Tiptoe* past the baby's room.
She *tiptoed* down the hall.
He was *tiptoeing* around the squeaky boards.
contrast: The *e* stays before *-ing*: *tiptoeing*.

transitivity: both — transitive (tour the museum), intransitive (the band tours in July)
gloss: To travel around a place, visiting the interesting parts.
examples: The band *tours* every summer.
We *toured* the old mission in the morning.
They are *touring* the national parks in a camper.

transitivity: transitive
gloss: To pull a vehicle or a boat behind another one.
examples: They will *tow* your car if you park here.
A pickup *towed* us to the shop.
His truck was *towing* a boat up the grade.
contrast: /toʊ/ rhymes with *go* and sounds exactly like *toe*.

transitivity: transitive
gloss: To follow the marks or signals that show where someone or something has gone.
examples: You can *track* the package online.
Rangers *tracked* the bear for two days.
We were *tracking* the storm all evening.

transitivity: both — transitive (trail the suspect), intransitive (the youngest kid trailed behind)
gloss: To follow slowly behind someone, or to hang down and drag along.
examples: The youngest kid always *trails* the group.
Two reporters *trailed* the bus all day.
Her scarf was *trailing* in the snow.

transitivity: both — transitive (transfer the patient), intransitive (transfer at Union Station)
gloss: To move from one place, vehicle, or line to another.
examples: You *transfer* at Union Station.
They *transferred* him to a hospital in the city.
We were *transferring* to another flight when the storm hit.
contrast: Stress falls on the last syllable, so the *r* doubles: *transferred, transferring*.

transitivity: transitive
gloss: To carry people or goods from one place to another.
examples: Trucks *transport* most of the grain.
The injured were *transported* by helicopter.
They are *transporting* the sculpture in three pieces.
contrast: The verb is stressed on the second syllable, trans-PORT; the noun is TRANS-port.

transitivity: both — transitive (travel the country), intransitive (they travel for work)
gloss: To go from one place to another, especially over a long distance.
examples: They *travel* for work about once a month.
We *traveled* through five states in a week.
She has been *traveling* since Tuesday.
contrast: American spelling keeps one *l*: *traveled, traveling, traveler* (British *travelled, travelling, traveller*).

transitivity: both — transitive (trip the runner), intransitive (he tripped on the step)
gloss: To catch your foot on something and lose your balance.
examples: Watch out or you will *trip*.
He *tripped* over the doorframe.
She was *tripping* on the hem of her coat all evening.
contrast: One vowel + one consonant, so the *p* doubles: *tripped, tripping*. Usually *trip **over*** something.

transitivity: intransitive
gloss: To fall or roll over suddenly and helplessly.
examples: Kids *tumble* down that hill all summer.
A rock *tumbled* down the slope.
Bags were *tumbling* off the cart.

transitivity: both — transitive (turn the wheel), intransitive (turn at the light)
gloss: To change direction, or to move something around a point.
examples: *Turn* left at the second light.
She *turned* the corner and disappeared.
The car ahead was *turning* without signaling.

transitivity: both — transitive (twist the cap), intransitive (the road twists)
gloss: To bend or curve in a changing direction, or to turn something with your hand.
examples: The road *twists* through the hills.
He *twisted* his ankle on the trail.
The path was *twisting* back on itself.

transitivity: both — transitive (unload the van), intransitive (we unloaded in the rain)
gloss: To take things off a vehicle or out of a container.
examples: Help me *unload* the van.
They *unloaded* the truck in the rain.
We were still *unloading* at midnight.

transitivity: both — transitive (unpack the suitcase), intransitive (I have not unpacked yet)
gloss: To take things out of a bag or a box after a trip.
examples: I have not had time to *unpack*.
She *unpacked* as soon as we got in.
He was *unpacking* when the phone rang.

transitivity: intransitive
gloss: To change direction suddenly, especially while moving.
examples: The trail *veers* right after the bridge.
The truck *veered* onto the shoulder.
A car was *veering* toward us.

transitivity: both — transitive (visit her parents), intransitive (they are just visiting)
gloss: To go to see a person or a place and spend some time there.
examples: We *visit* her parents every Thanksgiving.
They *visited* three cities in five days.
He has *visited* the museum twice this month.
contrast: Stress is on the first syllable, so the *t* is not doubled: *visited, visiting*.

transitivity: both — transitive (wade the creek), intransitive (we waded ashore)
gloss: To walk through water that is not deep.
examples: Herons *wade* along the shallow edge.
We *waded* across the creek.
She was *wading* out to the sandbar.

transitivity: both — transitive (walk the dog), intransitive (I walk to work)
gloss: To move on foot at a normal speed.
examples: I *walk* to work when it is dry.
We *walked* the last half mile.
He has been *walking* for two hours.
contrast: The *l* is silent: WAWK.

transitivity: both — transitive (wander the streets), intransitive (he wandered off)
gloss: To walk around slowly with no particular destination.
examples: He *wanders* off whenever we stop.
We *wandered* through the market all morning.
Tourists were *wandering* around the square.
contrast: *wander* /ˈwɑːndər/ (бродить) is not *wonder* /ˈwʌndər/ (удивляться, задаваться вопросом).

transitivity: both — transitive (yield the right of way), intransitive (yield to traffic in the circle)
gloss: To let other traffic go first.
examples: *Yield* to cars already in the circle.
He *yielded* to the truck coming down the ramp.
Drivers were not *yielding* at the crosswalk.
